fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. Jacob sees the angels and says, “This is the camp of God.” (Genesis 32:2) Then he names the place Mahanaim. Angels walk up on the road and the man stops to name the spot. I'd have dropped my whole tray, mustache and all.

Protector isn't in the message, friend. Jacob has the messengers say, “Your servant Jacob says…” and he calls Esau “…my master Esau…” (Genesis 32:4) Then the message goes on to list what Jacob has: oxen, donkeys, flocks, menservants and maidservants (Genesis 32:5). Not one word in it asks Esau to protect anybody.

True, baker. Jacob says he sent the message “…so that I may find favor in your sight.” (Genesis 32:5) Before that, he has the messengers tell Esau where he's been staying and what he has: oxen, donkeys, flocks, menservants and maidservants. The line about favor comes right after.

This one's true, friend. Jacob does give that reason: “…so that I may find favor in your sight.” (Genesis 32:5) He says it right after listing the oxen, donkeys, flocks, menservants and maidservants he has.
Armies sounds fitting, but the text says camps, friend. Jacob divides his people, flocks, herds and camels into two camps. (Genesis 32:7) Armies isn't the word that verse uses.

Escape, baker. Jacob thinks, “If Esau comes and attacks one camp, then the other camp can escape.” (Genesis 32:8) I think a man who just heard about four hundred men coming wants a way out built into his plan (Genesis 32:6). Two camps means everything isn't sitting in one spot.

That's the promise, baker. Jacob says, “But You have said, ‘I will surely make you prosper, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, too numerous to count.’” (Genesis 32:12) He brings God's own words right into his prayer. Next time you're at a beach, try counting the sand.

A gift, baker. Jacob spends the night there, and from what he had brought with him, he selects a gift for his brother Esau. (Genesis 32:13) He picks it out of his own animals, and the list starts with 200 female goats (Genesis 32:14). That's not a gift that fits in a bag.

That's his instruction, baker. Jacob entrusts the animals to his servants in separate herds and says, “Go on ahead of me, and keep some distance between the herds.” (Genesis 32:16) The herds go out ahead of him, each one separate, with room between them.

Right, baker. Jacob tells the lead servant what to say if Esau asks: “They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift, sent to my lord Esau.” (Genesis 32:18) The servant gets his answer ahead of time. And the name in it is Jacob's.
Laban is the man Jacob had been staying with (Genesis 32:4), but he isn't in this answer. The servant is to say, “They belong to your servant Jacob.” (Genesis 32:18) The animals are Jacob's gift.

Not quite, friend. Jacob thinks, “I will appease Esau with the gift that is going before me. After that I can face him, and perhaps he will accept me.” (Genesis 32:20) The word is perhaps. He's hoping, not sure.
